item.title: Peculiar Berakhot Part 1: The Three Categories of Blessings
item.description:
The Daily Halacha turns from parasha topics to a systematic series on lesser-known blessings that the Rabbis instituted on nature and life. This opening shiur recaps the three categories of berakhah: benefit, misvah, and praise or thanksgiving. It explains why recognising the category matters and that all these blessings are rabbinic.

item.title: Berakhot Part 2: Blessing HaShem on Seeing a Close Friend
item.description:
Is there a berakhah on seeing a close friend? If you have not seen a dear friend for 30 days you say Shehehiyanu, and after twelve months Mehayeh HaMetim, per the Gemara, Rambam and Tosafot. It applies equally to relatives, men or women, but only if you are truly happy to see them, and Shehehiyanu if you were in contact.

item.title: Berakhot Part 3: Blessings Upon Monkeys and Elephants
item.description:
What blessing do we say on seeing an elephant or a monkey? Baruch Meshaneh HaBeriyot, which the Shulhan Arukh limits to these two creatures, since the kipof is unclear. Sephardim say it once in a lifetime, and going to a zoo to say it is accepted practice, as Rav Haim Kanievsky did.

item.title: Berakhot Part 4: Blessing Upon Siamese Twins and the Diversity of the Human Race
item.description:
Is there a blessing on seeing a person born with a striking difference, such as a blind person, an amputee or Siamese twins? The Gemara and Shulhan Arukh say so. In practice it is said only for someone whose hardship you can feel, only for a Jew, and Sephardim say it once, while the Rema says every 30 days.

item.title: Berakhot Part 5: Blessing Upon Seeing an Exceptional חכם
item.description:
What berakhah do we say on seeing an exceptional Torah scholar? The Rambam, Rif, Rosh and Shulhan Arukh say a full blessing thanking God for giving of His wisdom to those who fear Him. The shiur explains that it is for a truly outstanding scholar in wisdom and character, not simply someone with many followers.

item.description:

item.title: Berakhot Part 7: Blessing Upon Seeing Royalty
item.description:
Is there a berakhah on seeing a king or a president? Yes, for a non-Jewish ruler, thanking God who gave of His glory to flesh and blood, and even a blind person may say it, as Rav Sheshet did. It applies to a ruler with real powers in royal or presidential pomp, and without God name if only the title remains.

item.title: Berakhot Part 8: Blessing Upon Seeing Beautiful Creatures
item.description:
What do we say on seeing a strikingly beautiful tree, animal or person? Shekakha Lo BaOlamo, that He has such things in His world, with God name. The Gemara tells of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who said it when he happened to pass a beautiful woman. Gazing is forbidden, but an unintended sight that astonishes you calls for the blessing.

item.title: Berakhot Part 9: Blessing Upon Seeing the Mediterranean Sea and the Oceans
item.description:
What blessing do we say on seeing the sea? Oseh Maaseh Bereshit on a regular sea, and a special one on the Yam HaGadol, if you have not seen it in 30 days. The Rishonim dispute whether that means the Mediterranean or the oceans, so the shiur suggests Sephardim say one and add the other straight after to cover both.

item.title: Berakhot Part 10: Blessing Upon the Dead Sea and Rivers
item.description:
Is there a blessing on the Dead Sea and on rivers? The Dead Sea has none, since Rashi says it was created after the destruction of Sedom, so it is not part of the work of creation. For rivers the Shulhan Arukh limits it to the four rivers of Bereshit, so Sephardim do not say it and Ashkenazim have a doubt.

item.title: Berakhot Part 11: Blessings Upon Mountains and Deserts
item.description:
What blessing do we say on mountains and deserts? Oseh Maaseh Bereshit, said with God name only for breathtaking mountains such as the Alps, Himalayas or Mount Hermon, and for vast inhabited deserts. The shiur adds that the 30-day rule applies to each type of phenomenon, so seeing two different ones close together calls for two blessings.

item.title: Berakhot Part 12: Blessings Upon Comets and Meteors
item.description:
What blessing do we say on seeing a comet or a meteor? The word zikin is understood either way, and the Gemara lets you choose between Oseh Maaseh Bereshit and the blessing on His might and strength. Because they pass quickly, it must be said within a few seconds of seeing them, unlike mountains or seas.

item.title: Berakhot Part 13 Blessings Upon Earthquakes and Hurricanes & Strong Winds
item.description:
Is there a berakhah on an earthquake or a strong wind? The Mishnah lists a blessing on zeaot, an earthquake, and on very strong winds such as a hurricane or tornado, and you choose Oseh Maaseh Bereshit or Shekohoh UGevurato Maleh Olam. Say it within seconds, with no 30-day rule, and again once your attention has moved on.

item.title: Berakhot Part 14: Blessings Upon Lightning and Thunder
item.description:
Are there two different blessings for lightning and thunder? No, it is a common mistake. The Gemara, Rambam and Shulhan Arukh give one blessing on seeing lightning or hearing thunder, chosen from the same two as for earthquakes, to be said within a few seconds. If you wake at night, you may rub your hands and say it before washing.

item.title: Berakhot Part 15: Blessings Upon Rainbows
item.description:
What do we say on seeing a rainbow, and should we tell others? We say Zokher HaBerit, thanking God who remembers His covenant not to destroy the world. The Rabbis advise against gazing at it, out of respect. The Hayei Adam says not to tell others, which some Ashkenazim follow, but Sephardim do tell others so they may say it.

item.title: Berakhot Part 18: Blessing Upon a Place Where a Miracle Occurred to an Individual
item.description:
What if a miracle happened to you in a certain place? Each time you return, after 30 days away, say Shehasah Li Nes BaMakom HaZeh, and your children and grandchildren say it for their parents and grandparents. A miracle here means surviving where most people would have died, such as an attack or being trapped, not an ordinary escape.

item.description:

It is said once in 30 days, but again at a different cemetery or after new burials. The Gemara gives two reasons for visiting graves on fast days.

item.title: Berakhot Part 20: Blessing on the Moon
item.description:
What are the common misconceptions about Kiddush Levanah, the blessing on the moon? It is said on the monthly renewal of the moon, and many Rishonim allow it from the first days of the month. It can be said when the moon is clearly visible through some cloud, and the Psalm and verses around it were added because it is like greeting the Shekhinah.

item.title: Berakhot Part 21: Blessings Upon Joyous and Not So Joyous Occasions in Life
item.description:
Which blessings did the Rabbis institute for the joyful and painful moments of life? They express that everything comes from the one God. Shehehiyanu is said when only one person benefits, and HaTov VeHametiv when joy is shared by more than one, for example a lottery win that goes into a joint account of husband and wife.

item.title: Berakhot Part 22: Shehiyanu on Various Items
item.description:
What do we say Shehehiyanu on? The Mishnah, Rambam and Shulhan Arukh name a new house, new furniture or utensils, and new garments, including shoes if you are truly happy with them. Clothes are personal and always take Shehehiyanu, while shared items such as a house or furniture used jointly take HaTov VeHametiv.

item.title: Berakhot Part 23: Blessing on New House
item.description:
Should you say Shehehiyanu on a new house? The Mishnah, Gemara and Shulhan Arukh say yes, when you buy it and move in, though not for a rental. The Ben Ish Hai records a custom not to say it, so it is said together with a new garment or fruit, but the shiur argues it is a pity to lose such a berakhah.

item.title: Berakhot Part 24: Blessings on Good and Not So Good Tidings
item.description:
What do we say on hearing good news, and on hearing bad news? Exceptionally good news for yourself calls for Shehehiyanu, and good news benefiting others calls for HaTov VeHametiv. Hearing very bad news calls for Dayan HaEmet, with no distinction between individual and many, and the shiur ends on the Rabbis marking both good and bad times with berakhot.
